chapter_title: Introduction to C# Scripting for XR Interactions

screens.title: Introduction to C# Scripting for XR Interactions
screens.subtitle: Using C# and MonoBehaviour to give GameObjects behavior, respond to input, and move reliably across frames.

narration.text: In this chapter we bring GameObjects to life by writing C# scripts that run inside Unity. You will learn why every runtime script attached to an object inherits from MonoBehaviour, and how that inheritance grants access to lifecycle hooks, the transform component, and the engine's input system. We'll make a small mover script, explore the difference between one-time initialization and per-frame updates, and see how Time. deltaTime lets movement feel the same on slow and fast machines. You will also learn how public variables and the SerializeField attribute expose values to the Inspector so designers can tweak behavior without editing code. Along the way we'll practice simple input checks using the Input class, which provides the same foundation you'll later use for controller and gesture input in XR. By the end of these slides you'll be able to attach a script, move a cube with keyboard tests, and avoid common mistakes like forgetting to check for null references or leaving heavy work inside the per-frame Update. Think about a virtual button in your scene — with these basics you can make it respond reliably and smoothly.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: C# scripts inheriting from MonoBehaviour connect your code to Unity's lifecycle, transform access, and input system — the building blocks for XR interactions.

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.subtitle: Four concrete skills to practice while writing your first XR interaction scripts.

narration.text: By the end of these exercises you will be able to create a C# script that attaches to a GameObject, initialize it for runtime, move it reliably, and read simple input for testing. First, you will understand the role of MonoBehaviour and the automatic lifecycle that Unity uses to call Start and Update. Second, you will learn when to place one-time setup code in Start versus continuous logic in Update or physics code in FixedUpdate. Third, you will be able to declare public variables and use the SerializeField attribute so values appear in the Inspector for rapid iteration. Fourth, you will write code that manipulates transform. position and transform. Translate along with Time. deltaTime so movement remains consistent across frame rates. Each objective is paired with a small visual mnemonic to reinforce the mental model: lifecycle steps, inspector knobs, transform axes, and delta-time smoothing. These skills matter because they form the basis of all XR interactions — from moving objects to responding to controller input — and they reduce bugs like missing references or choppy motion. As you work through the hands-on mover activity, try to explain aloud why Time. deltaTime is used; that reflection will help cement the habit.

keyIdea.title: Practical outcomes
keyIdea.text: Initialize components safely, expose tweakable fields, move objects frame-independently, and capture input for prototypes.

screens.title: How you'll practice these skills
screens.subtitle: Concrete activities and checks to make scripting in Unity safe and testable.

narration.text: In practical work you'll create a Mover script, attach it to a cube, and test movement with keyboard input — a simple but powerful loop: code, attach, run, adjust. Start by creating a Scripts folder and a C# script named Mover. Use Start to print a debug message and set an initial position so you can confirm the script ran. Implement Update to read Input. GetKey for W and S and Translate the transform forward or back, and Input. GetKey for A and D to rotate the object. Make speed a public float so you can vary it in the Inspector without recompiling. When testing, use Debug. Log in Start and Update to observe the call order in the Console: Start runs once, then Update runs every frame. Also try changing Speed while the scene runs; public values update live and that's a fast iteration technique. Finally, add null checks when you reference other GameObjects to avoid NullReferenceException. These activities build good habits: always confirm initialization, keep heavy computations out of Update, and use inspector-visible fields to iterate quickly.

screens.title: C# scripts and MonoBehaviour
screens.subtitle: What it means for a script to inherit from MonoBehaviour and why that matters in Unity.

narration.text: A C# script in Unity becomes a component when it inherits from MonoBehaviour. That inheritance is not decorative — it is the engine's contract that lets Unity call your methods at specific times and grant your code access to common APIs like transform, Start, Update, and the Input system. When you attach a MonoBehaviour script to a GameObject, Unity constructs a component instance that can read and write that GameObject's Transform, access other components via GetComponent, and receive lifecycle callbacks. A concrete example: if you write public class MyMover : MonoBehaviour, and attach it to a Cube, calling transform. Translate inside Update moves that Cube because transform points to that Cube's Transform component. A common misconception is to think a plain static class or a class that does not inherit will be executed; it will not be invoked by Unity as a component. Also, MonoBehaviour methods like Start are only called when the component is enabled. Finally, remember that MonoBehaviour provides convenience, not magic: you still manage references, check for nulls, and avoid expensive work in per-frame methods. Consider what must run only once versus repeatedly, and keep initialization separate from continuous updates.

keyIdea.title: MonoBehaviour role
keyIdea.text: Inheritance connects your code to Unity's component system and lifecycle, enabling per-object behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › C# scripts & MonoBehaviour
Definition

What MonoBehaviour provides

MonoBehaviour is the base class that registers your script as a component Unity can manage. It exposes lifecycle hooks, transform access, and component utilities.

Concrete example
Attach public class MyMover : MonoBehaviour to a Cube. Inside Update, calling transform.Translate moves that specific Cube each frame.
Common misconception
A plain C# class not inheriting MonoBehaviour will not be treated as a component and won't receive Start or Update calls from Unity.
Key Takeaway

MonoBehaviour is the bridge that lets Unity call your methods and give your script access to the GameObject's components.

Inspect this
Component behaviors
  • transform property points to the GameObject's Transform component.
  • GetComponent() retrieves sibling components on the same GameObject.
  • Enabled components receive Start and Update; disabled ones do not.
Check your understanding
Why must you check for null when you store references to other objects? Answer: those references may not be assigned or the object may be missing at runtime, causing runtime exceptions.

screens.title: Start(), Update(), and FixedUpdate lifecycle
screens.subtitle: When Unity calls these methods and how to use them appropriately.

narration.text: Unity invokes specific MonoBehaviour methods at predictable times. Start is called once, just before the first frame update, and is ideal for initialization that depends on other objects already being set up. Update is called every frame and should contain per-frame logic such as reading input or triggering animations. FixedUpdate runs on a fixed timestep and is intended for physics-related updates to ensure consistent simulation. A concrete example: use Start to cache references to components or position a GameObject at its initial place; use Update to poll Input. GetKey and apply transform. Translate; and use FixedUpdate to apply Rigidbody forces for physics-driven movement. A common mistake is putting heavy computations or allocations inside Update — that can cause frame drops and jitter, which are especially problematic in VR where low and stable frame rates are essential for comfort. Another misconception is to assume Update frequency is stable; instead, rely on Time. deltaTime to scale motion in Update to the actual frame interval. Ask yourself: does this code need a fixed physics timestep, or is a per-frame update sufficient? Choosing correctly preserves stability and predictability.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle choice
keyIdea.text: Use Start for one-time setup, Update for per-frame checks, and FixedUpdate for physics to keep behavior consistent.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Lifecycle Methods
Overview

Start, Update, FixedUpdate

Understand when Unity calls each method so you can place initialization, input checks, and physics updates correctly.
Start()
Called once before the first frame. Ideal for getting references and initial state.
Update()
Called every frame. Use for reading input and non-physics movement, scaling by Time.deltaTime.
FixedUpdate()
Called on a fixed timestep for physics calculations and consistent simulation results.
Key Takeaway

Place one-time initialization in Start, per-frame logic in Update (scaled by delta time), and physics updates in FixedUpdate.

Quick guide
Example scenario
Start: set initial health and find the main camera. Update: rotate an object in response to input. FixedUpdate: apply forces to a Rigidbody to simulate realistic collisions.
Performance note
Expensive per-frame work causes dropped frames. In VR this leads to discomfort, so profile and move heavy tasks off of Update.
Misconception check
Update runs at variable intervals. Always multiply motion by Time.deltaTime instead of assuming a fixed frame rate.

screens.title: Variables, public fields, and [SerializeField]
screens.subtitle: How to declare data in C# scripts and expose it to the Unity Inspector safely.

narration.text: Variables store the data your script needs: numbers, references to other GameObjects, flags, and more. In Unity, marking a field public makes it appear in the Inspector, which is extremely useful for tuning gameplay values without recompiling. If you prefer to keep a field private but still editable in the Inspector, use the [SerializeField] attribute. For example, public float moveSpeed = 5.0f appears as a numeric field you can change at runtime. A common workflow is to keep fields private by default and add [SerializeField] only for values you want designers to tweak. Always be cautious about exposing references to other GameObjects: if a referenced object is removed or not assigned, your script may throw a NullReferenceException at runtime. Practice defensive checks, for example ensuring targetObject!= null before calling its transform. Another subtle point is that changing field values in the Inspector during Play mode updates them immediately, but those changes are not permanent unless you explicitly save them after stopping Play. This live-tuning ability speeds iteration, so prefer inspector-visible fields for frequently adjusted parameters like speed, jump height, or effect intensities.

keyIdea.title: Inspector-friendly fields
keyIdea.text: Use public or [SerializeField] fields to expose tweakable parameters while guarding against null references.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Variables & Inspector
Declaration

Public vs [SerializeField]

Public fields show in the Inspector. [SerializeField] exposes private fields while keeping encapsulation in code.

Example
public float moveSpeed = 5.0f;
[SerializeField] private GameObject targetObject;
Common mistake
Not assigning references in the Inspector leads to NullReferenceException. Always check for null before using external objects.
Practical tips
  • Keep fields private by default; expose what needs tweaking with [SerializeField].
  • Use clear names like moveSpeed or targetObject so it's obvious in the Inspector.
  • Remember Inspector changes during Play are temporary; copy values back if you want them persistent.
Key Takeaway

Expose tweakable fields to speed iteration, and protect against null references when using assigned GameObjects.

screens.title: The transform property and object manipulation
screens.subtitle: How transform gives programmatic control over position, rotation, and scale.

narration.text: Every GameObject owns a Transform component, and Unity exposes it directly via the transform property inside MonoBehaviour scripts. This property is your primary handle for changing position, rotation, and scale in code. For absolute placement use transform. position = new Vector3(x, y, z). For relative motion, use transform. Translate with a direction vector multiplied by speed and Time. deltaTime. To rotate an object, call transform. Rotate with an axis and a value multiplied by delta time. The transform A P I is simple but powerful, and it's important to choose the right approach: setting position replaces the absolute location, while Translate moves relative to the object's orientation. A concrete example: moving a Cube forward in local space uses transform. Translate(Vector3. forward * speed * Time. deltaTime). A common misconception is that direct assignment ignores frame timing; in Update you must multiply by Time. deltaTime so movement is frame-rate independent. Also be careful when mixing transform changes with physics-driven Rigidbody movement — if physics controls position, apply forces on the Rigidbody instead of directly setting Transform to avoid conflicts. The core idea: use transform for direct visual motion and respect the simulation context when physics are involved.

keyIdea.title: Transform control
keyIdea.text: Use transform.position for absolute placement and transform.Translate/Rotate for relative, frame-independent motion.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Transform & Manipulation
API

Position, Rotation, Scale

Access transform to set absolute positions or move relative to an object's forward vector.
Examples
// Absolute
transform.position = new Vector3(0f, 1f, 0f);

// Relative
transform.Translate(Vector3.forward * speed * Time.deltaTime);

// Rotation
transform.Rotate(0, 90 * Time.deltaTime, 0);
Physics note
If a Rigidbody controls motion, prefer Rigidbody methods over directly setting Transform to avoid simulation conflicts.
Practice
Try this
Set a Cube at Y = 0.5 in Start, then use Update to translate forward with W and back with S while rotating with A and D.
Misconception
Using Translate without Time.deltaTime will make movement dependent on frame-rate, causing different speeds on different machines.
Key Takeaway

Choose absolute or relative transform methods deliberately and scale motion by delta time for consistent behavior.

screens.title: Time.deltaTime and frame-rate independent movement
screens.subtitle: Why multiplying by Time.deltaTime keeps object motion consistent across devices.

narration.text: Time. deltaTime is the duration, in seconds, of the previous frame. When you multiply movement by Time. deltaTime inside Update, you convert a per-frame delta into a per-second rate. This means that an object moving at five units per second travels about the same distance whether the game runs at 30 frames per second or 120 frames per second. Concrete example: transform. Translate(Vector3. forward * speed * Time. deltaTime) moves forward at speed units per second. Without this multiplier, motion scales with frame count and will appear faster on higher frame rates. A common error is forgetting delta time when prototyping, which often goes unnoticed on the developer's machine but shows up on other hardware or in VR headsets, causing uncomfortable inconsistencies. Another important point is that FixedUpdate uses a fixed delta time that Unity manages, so physics should be updated inside FixedUpdate and scaled by Time. fixedDeltaTime when necessary. When profiling, prefer using simple multipliers and keep heavy loops out of Update. To test your understanding, change speed in the Inspector during Play and notice how the mover preserves a steady velocity if your code uses Time. deltaTime correctly.

keyIdea.title: Frame-rate independence
keyIdea.text: Multiply per-frame changes by Time.deltaTime so behavior represents units per second, not per frame.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Time.deltaTime
Concept

Use delta time for stable motion

Scaling by Time.deltaTime converts per-frame deltas into per-second rates so movement is consistent across machines.
Code snippet
void Update()
{
    if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.W))
    {
        transform.Translate(Vector3.forward * speed * Time.deltaTime);
    }
}
Misconception
Assuming fixed frame timing leads to faster movement on high-refresh hardware; always use delta time unless working with fixed timesteps.
Practice
Test idea
Run on machines with different frame rates or change Editor Quality settings to confirm consistent movement when using Time.deltaTime.
FixedUpdate note
For physics operations use FixedUpdate and Time.fixedDeltaTime to align with Unity's fixed timestep.
Key Takeaway

Multiply motion by Time.deltaTime to express speed in units per second and keep movement stable across frames.

screens.title: Detecting input with the Input class
screens.subtitle: Basic methods for keyboard and mouse checks used in prototyping XR interactions.

narration.text: Unity's Input class provides simple, synchronous checks for keyboard and mouse which are ideal for testing and debugging XR interactions on desktop. Key methods include Input. GetKey which returns true while a key is held, Input. GetKeyDown which returns true on the frame the key was pressed, and Input. GetKeyUp which returns true on the frame the key was released. For mouse input, Input. GetMouseButton(0) checks the left button state. A concrete example: using if (Input. GetKey(KeyCode. W)) inside Update moves an object forward as long as the key is held. Contrast this with GetKeyDown which is perfect for one-shot actions like toggling a UI element when the key is pressed once. A common pitfall is checking for GetKeyDown inside FixedUpdate — because FixedUpdate runs on a different timing, input checks are best placed in Update to capture frame events reliably. These simple checks are a foundation; later when working with XR hardware you'll replace or augment them with controller input APIs, but the mental model of polling input each frame remains the same. Always consider input sampling frequency and where to place your checks for predictable behavior.

keyIdea.title: Input basics
keyIdea.text: Use GetKey for held states, GetKeyDown for single-frame presses, and GetMouseButton for mouse checks while prototyping.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Input Detection
API Reference

Input.GetKey / GetKeyDown / GetKeyUp

Poll keyboard and mouse states inside Update to react to held keys or single presses.
Examples
// Held
if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.W)) { /* move forward while held */ }

// Pressed this frame
if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.E)) { /* trigger once */ }

// Released this frame
if (Input.GetKeyUp(KeyCode.E)) { /* on release */ }
Notes
Where to check
Perform input checks in Update for consistent per-frame sampling. Avoid relying on FixedUpdate for input events.
Use case
Use keyboard checks for rapid prototyping. Later swap to XR controller input without changing the concept of per-frame polling.
Misconception
GetKeyDown detects the press only in the single frame it occurred; don't use it for continuous actions like walking forward.
Key Takeaway

Choose the correct input check for the intended behavior: hold, press-once, or release events.

screens.title: Hands-on: The Mover script walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Step through the provided Mover script, attach it, and test keyboard-driven motion.

narration.text: Let's walk through the m over script you'll implement. The script begins with public float speed = 5.0f so you can change movement in the Inspector. In Start you may call Debug. Log to confirm the script executed and optionally set transform. position to the starting place. In Update the code checks Input. GetKey for W and S to translate forward and back, and checks A and D to rotate using transform. Rotate. Notice each movement multiplies by Time. deltaTime to ensure frame-rate independence. A concrete hands-on flow: create a Cube, add a Scripts folder, create Mover. cs, replace the template with the supplied code, save and drag the script onto the Cube. Enter Play mode, press W to move forward and D to rotate. Try changing Speed in the Inspector while running to see live updates. Watch for errors in the Console — if targetObject or other references are null, add a null check before calling transform on them. This practice shows how lifecycle, variables, transforms, delta-time, and input combine into a functional prototype. After testing, reflect: which parts run only once and which run every frame?

keyIdea.title: Combine concepts
keyIdea.text: The Mover script demonstrates lifecycle, inspector fields, transform manipulation, delta-time, and input checks in one practical example.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Mover Walkthrough
Starter code
using UnityEngine;

public class Mover : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float speed = 5.0f;

    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("Mover script started!");
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.W))
        {
            transform.Translate(Vector3.forward * speed * Time.deltaTime);
        }

        if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.S))
        {
            transform.Translate(Vector3.back * speed * Time.deltaTime);
        }

        if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.A))
        {
            transform.Rotate(0, -90 * Time.deltaTime, 0);
        }

        if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.D))
        {
            transform.Rotate(0, 90 * Time.deltaTime, 0);
        }
    }
}
Attachment & Test
Create a Cube at X:0 Y:0.5 Z:0, attach Mover, press Play, and use W,A,S,D to move and rotate. Watch the Console for the Debug.Log message from Start to confirm the script ran.
Live tweaking
Change speed in the Inspector during Play to observe immediate effects. Remember those Play-mode edits are temporary unless saved.
Common error
NullReferenceException occurs when references aren't assigned. Add checks like if (targetObject != null) before using it.
Reflection prompt
Which lines run once and which lines run every frame? Why does that distinction matter for initialization and performance?
Key Takeaway

This script ties together lifecycle, inspector fields, transforms, delta-time, and input to form a working prototype you can iterate on.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.subtitle: How to spot and fix frequent runtime issues when scripting interactions.

narration.text: When scripting interactions you will encounter a few recurring issues. One is NullReferenceException, usually caused by an unassigned GameObject or component reference. The fix is to assign the reference in the Inspector or add defensive checks before usage. Another is forgetting to multiply by Time. deltaTime, which makes movement frame-dependent and inconsistent across devices. A third is performing expensive operations inside Update, like heavy loops or allocations, which harms frame rate and can cause motion sickness in VR. To debug: use Debug. Log in Start and Update to confirm execution order and watched values, check the Console for exceptions, and verify Inspector-assigned fields before Play. Compare approaches: direct transform assignments are simple for visual-only objects, but if physics drives an object use Rigidbody APIs inside FixedUpdate. Also remember input sampling should occur in Update; using FixedUpdate for input can miss frame events. A practical tip: when you see jitters, first check where you change transforms and whether those changes respect delta time and physics ownership. This structured troubleshooting habit will make your XR prototypes more stable and comfortable. Common mistakes and debugging tips means check for null references, scale motion by delta time, avoid heavy per-frame work, and match movement method to physics ownership.. In practical terms, how to spot and fix frequent runtime issues when scripting interactions.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debugging habits
keyIdea.text: Check for null references, scale motion by delta time, avoid heavy per-frame work, and match movement method to physics ownership.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Common Mistakes
Typical errors
NullReferenceException
Ensure inspector fields are assigned or add if (target != null) checks before use.
Missing Time.deltaTime
Movement without delta time varies by frame rate; always scale per-frame changes by delta time.
Heavy Update work
Move expensive calculations off Update or cache results to avoid frame drops.
Debugging checklist
  1. Confirm Start runs with Debug.Log to validate attachment.
  2. Inspect assigned fields in the Inspector before Play.
  3. Check Console for exceptions and stack traces to locate missing references.
  4. Profile Update to find costly operations and move them out or cache results.
Developer tip
Add small Debug.Logs and temporarily lower quality settings to reproduce performance issues quickly on your development machine.
Key Takeaway

Follow the checklist: verify initialization, inspector assignments, delta-time usage, and move heavy work away from Update to keep XR experiences stable.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Six compact reminders of the most important terms and ideas.

narration.text: Let's distill the chapter into concise reminders you can recall while coding. First, a C# script is a file that defines behavior and becomes a component when attached to a GameObject. Second, MonoBehaviour is the base class that grants the script access to Unity's lifecycle and utilities. Third, Start is used for one-time initialization tasks before the first frame. Fourth, Update is called every frame and is the place for continuous checks such as input polling and non-physics movement. Fifth, Time. deltaTime represents the time of the last frame and must multiply per-frame motion to express speed in units per second. Sixth, the Input class provides methods like GetKey and GetKeyDown to detect held and single-frame key events. Keep these six ideas in mind as you build prototypes: they form the minimal vocabulary for attaching logic, moving objects, and responding to user actions in Unity.

keyIdea.title: Quick reference
keyIdea.text: These terms form the foundation of scripting interactions and should guide decisions while prototyping.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts — Part 1

C# Script
File that defines behavior attached to GameObjects.
MonoBehaviour
Base class that connects scripts to Unity's engine and lifecycle.
Start()
Called once before the first frame for initialization tasks.
Update()
Called every frame; suitable for input and frame-based motion.
Time.deltaTime
Seconds since last frame; use to make motion rate-based instead of frame-based.
Input class
Provides GetKey, GetKeyDown, and mouse checks for prototyping input.
Summary
Keep these core terms handy as you prototype: scripts, MonoBehaviour, Start, Update, delta time, and basic input.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Three final reminders and a short takeaway to close the chapter.

narration.text: To finish, remember transform for direct position and rotation control, the [SerializeField] attribute to expose private fields in the Inspector, and the practical habit of separating initialization from per-frame code. Transform gives you programmatic control over position, rotation, and scale, which you will use constantly to position visual elements and animate simple interactions. [SerializeField] lets you keep implementation details private while still exposing tuning knobs to designers. Finally, adopt the pattern of initializing in Start, reading input and moving in Update, and using FixedUpdate for physics so your code is predictable and performant. These three practices reduce bugs, speed iteration, and result in smoother XR experiences. As a closing reflection, think about how you would convert keyboard-based input in your mover into an XR controller input: the polling idea stays the same, but you will query controller axes or button states instead of keyboard keys.

keyIdea.title: Final takeaway
keyIdea.text: Combine transforms, inspector-visible fields, and lifecycle discipline to build stable, tweakable XR interactions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts — Part 2

transform
Programmatic access to position, rotation, and scale for direct manipulation.
[SerializeField]
Expose private fields to the Inspector so you can tune values without changing code access modifiers.
Lifecycle discipline
Put initialization in Start, input and motion in Update, and physics in FixedUpdate for predictability.
Chapter summary
These patterns make your XR prototypes easier to build, tune, and debug. Practice converting keyboard tests to XR controller input to continue progressing.
